\chapter{Greetings and the First Devanagari Runway}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Marathi, move \mr{हो} from tracing through dictation, and read \mr{नमस्कार} by assembling only signs I have already practised.}

Read \mr{नमस्कार}, write \mr{हो} without a visible model, and retrieve the six-word greeting, response, thanks, and leave-taking exchange in one short final checkpoint.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[namaskar]{\mr{नमस्कार} (namaskār) — \textquotedblleft{}greetings\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-namaskar}



\begin{quote}
The first Marathi word — and the everyday greeting of Maharashtra.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(If you already read Devanagari, skim this.)} Devanagari runs \textbf{left to right}; every consonant carries a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\mr{न}} na, \textbf{\mr{म}} ma, \textbf{\mr{का}} kā, \textbf{\mr{र}} ra. The stroke under \textbf{\mr{स्}} (a \emph{halant}) removes its vowel, so the bare \emph{s} leans onto the next as a conjunct: \textbf{\mr{स्} + \mr{का} $\to$ \mr{स्का}}. Read \textbf{\mr{न}·\mr{म}·\mr{स्}·\mr{का}·\mr{र}} $\to$ \textbf{namaskār}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}} (\emph{namaskār}) = \textbf{\mr{नमः}} (\emph{namaḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{कार}} (\emph{kāra}, \textquotedblleft{}the making of\textquotedblright{}), from Sanskrit — literally \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow.\textquotedblright{} The same word Kannada and Telugu borrowed, and close kin to Hindi's \emph{namaskār}. But note: where Hindi leans on \emph{namaste}, Marathi's default, all-purpose greeting is \textbf{namaskār} — one of many small ways the two Devanagari languages differ.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Said with palms pressed together, respectful and neutral — hello and goodbye, any time, to almost anyone. Warmer and more casual: \emph{kāy mhaṇtā?} (\textquotedblleft{}what do you say?\textquotedblright{} $\approx$ \textquotedblleft{}how's it going?\textquotedblright{}) among friends.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read it — na · ma · s · kā · r $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}namaskār\textquotedblright{}
  \item what a \emph{halant} does (removes \mr{स}'s vowel, for the \mr{स्का} conjunct)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}} literally mean, and how does Marathi's greeting habit differ from Hindi's? (\textquotedblleft{}The making of a bow\textquotedblright{}; Marathi favors \emph{namaskār}, Hindi \emph{namaste}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ha]{\mr{ह} — the consonant ha}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ha}



\begin{quote}
Nothing is assumed but the words you can already say. This chapter turns them into words you can read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Devanagari is an \textbf{abugida}, and that word carries the whole system.

It is not an alphabet, where each letter is one sound. It is a system where \textbf{a consonant already carries a vowel}, and you write a vowel mark only when you want a different one.

Here is the first consonant:

\begin{quote}
\mr{ह}
\end{quote}

That is not \emph{h}. It is \textbf{ha} — the consonant \emph{h} with an \textbf{a} already inside it, the \emph{a} of English \emph{about}. Nobody wrote that vowel. A bare consonant in this script is understood to carry it, and it is called the \textbf{inherent vowel}.

Now look at the top of the shape. There is a \textbf{horizontal bar} running across it, and it is not decoration. It is the \textbf{shirorekhā}, the head-line, and in running Devanagari it joins up across a whole word so the writing appears to hang from a washing line. It is the single most recognisable thing about this script — and Gujarati, its sister, is written by \textbf{erasing} exactly this line.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace one consonant}
Keep \textbf{\mr{ह}} visible. Finger-trace it once, then trace one printed model once with a pencil. Say \emph{ha} only after your hand stops. Do not copy the word for \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} yet; its vowel sign comes next.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel does a bare consonant carry? (\textbf{a} — the inherent vowel, and nobody writes it.) What is the bar across the top called, and what does it do in a whole word? (The \textbf{shirorekhā}; it \textbf{joins up} across the word.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-o]{\mr{ो} — the vowel sign that replaces the inherent a}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-o-matra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
The inherent \textbf{a} is a default. To get a different vowel you \textbf{replace} it, with a mark called a \textbf{mātrā}.

\begin{quote}
\mr{ो}
\end{quote}

On its own it is meaningless. Attached to a consonant it swaps the inherent short \emph{a} for \textbf{o}, the vowel of English \emph{go} — and notice how it attaches: a stroke to the right, plus a small mark \textbf{riding on the head-line itself}.

Put it on the consonant you have:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{ह}} + \textbf{\mr{ो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{हो}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ho.} That is a word: it is \textbf{yes}, and you have been saying it since your first lesson in Marathi.

One consonant and one mark, and a word you could already say became a word you can \textbf{read}. Nothing was memorised as a picture.

\subsection*{Writing — one supported copy}
Keep \textbf{\mr{हो}} visible. Copy it once: first \textbf{\mr{ह}}, then its attached \textbf{\mr{ो}} sign. Point to both pieces in your copy and read \emph{ho}. You may look back after each piece; memory is not the task yet.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a mātrā do to the inherent vowel? (\textbf{Replaces} it.) What word did those two pieces make? (\textbf{\mr{हो}} — \emph{ho}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ho]{\mr{हो} — look, hide, write, compare}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ho-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Look at \textbf{\mr{हो}} for five seconds. Point first to \textbf{\mr{ह}}, then to attached \textbf{\mr{ो}}. Do not copy it while the model is visible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
1. cover \textbf{\mr{हो}} 2. wait five seconds 3. write it once from memory 4. uncover the model and compare the two pieces

If one piece differs, circle it and repair only that place. Repair is part of the exercise, not a failure. There is no tracing and no romanized answer model.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read your repaired word as \emph{ho}. Stop after one memory attempt.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ho]{One heard answer — write what you know}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ho-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover the answer lower on this page. You will hear one familiar answer. No new Marathi and no new Devanagari shape is hiding in this lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — short dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{ho} — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}{]}

Write the Devanagari word from sound alone. Do not use a visible model, romanization, or tracing guide. Now uncover and compare: \textbf{\mr{हो}}. Check \textbf{\mr{ह}} first and attached \textbf{\mr{ो}} second. Repair one place if needed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Writing from sound completes this tiny runway. It is not a mock assessment; later lessons must grow from one known word to forms, messages, and timed tasks.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\mr{न} — the consonant na}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-na}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{न}
\end{quote}

\textbf{na}, with the same inherent \textbf{a} inside it — the \emph{n} of English \emph{net}, then the vowel nobody wrote.

Nothing new in the machinery. This is simply another consonant, and every rule you already have applies to it unchanged. That is the payoff of learning the system rather than the words: \textbf{every consonant from here behaves exactly like the two you already know.} New shapes are coming; new rules are not.

Write it beside the first, and notice both hang from the same head-line.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{न}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel is inside \textbf{\mr{न}} when nothing is attached? (\textbf{a}.) And how many new rules did this lesson introduce? (\textbf{None} — only a shape.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ā]{\mr{ा} — a second vowel sign, and the simplest one in the script}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-aa-matra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ा}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ā}, the long \emph{a} of English \emph{father}. It is a single upright stroke standing to the \textbf{right} of its consonant, dropping from the head-line.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{न}} + \textbf{\mr{ा}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{ना}}
\end{quote}

\emph{nā}. One beat — a mātrā changes the vowel, it never adds a beat.

You now hold two vowel signs, and they sit in different places: one to the right with a mark above, one plainly to the right. \textbf{Where a mātrā sits is part of its identity}, not a style choice, and in this family of scripts they can go right, left, above, below, or on both sides at once. A reader learns to look \textbf{around} a consonant rather than only after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{ा}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does this mātrā sit? (To the \textbf{right} of the consonant.) Does it add a beat? (\textbf{No} — it replaces the vowel.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ī]{\mr{ी} — a mātrā that leans the other way}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ii-matra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ी}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ī}, the long \emph{ee} of English \emph{see}. It stands to the right like the last one, but with a curve that rises and \textbf{hooks back over the head-line to the left}.

Here it is, and here is what it completes:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{ह}} + \textbf{\mr{ी}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{ही}}
\end{quote}

And now put that beside a piece you already built:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{ना}} + \textbf{\mr{ही}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{नाही}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{nā-hī} — \textbf{no}.

You can now read both answers to a yes-or-no question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{हो}}   \textbf{\mr{नाही}}
\end{quote}

Two consonants and three vowel signs. That is the arithmetic of an abugida: consonants and mātrās \textbf{multiply}, so a small number of pieces reaches a large number of syllables very fast.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{ी}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\mr{नाही}}? (\textbf{No}.) How many pieces is it built from? (\textbf{Four} — two consonants and two mātrās.) And which two mātrās look similar but hook differently? (The \textbf{ā} and the \textbf{ī}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ma]{\mr{म} — the consonant ma}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ma}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{म}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ma} — the \emph{m} of English \emph{met}, with the inherent vowel riding along.

Three consonants now. Say them in the order you met them, each with the vowel nobody wrote:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{ह}}   \textbf{\mr{न}}   \textbf{\mr{म}}
\end{quote}

\emph{ha, na, ma.} Three shapes, one head-line each, and the same rule under all of them.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{म}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the three consonants you hold, each with its inherent vowel. (\emph{\textbf{ha, na, ma}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sa]{\mr{स} — the consonant sa}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-sa}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{स}
\end{quote}

\textbf{sa} — the \emph{s} of English \emph{sit}, plus the inherent vowel.

Four consonants. You are most of the way to a word you have been saying since your very first lesson, and the only piece of machinery still missing is the one that handles two consonants pressed together.

\subsection*{Your turn}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the inherent vowel in \textbf{\mr{स}}? (\textbf{a} — \emph{sa}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.

\section[ka]{\mr{क} — the consonant ka}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ka}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{क}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ka} — the \emph{k} of English \emph{skip}, unaspirated, with no puff of breath after it.

Hold your palm in front of your mouth and say English \emph{kit}: you feel air. Say \emph{skip}: you do not. \textbf{This is the second one.} Devanagari has a separate letter for the breathy version, and swapping them changes the word — so the difference that English treats as an accident is one this script writes down.

Five consonants, two mātrās, and one thing left.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{क}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\mr{क}} the \emph{k} of \emph{kit} or of \emph{skip}? (Of \emph{\textbf{skip}} — no puff of air.) And does the script care? (\textbf{Yes} — the breathy one is a different letter.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(virama)]{\mr{्} — the mark that DELETES the inherent vowel and glues two consonants together}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-virama}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
The inherent vowel is a nuisance when you do not want it. If a word presses two consonants together with no vowel between them, writing them plainly would insert an \emph{a} that is not there.

So there is a mark that \textbf{removes} it:

\begin{quote}
\mr{्}
\end{quote}

This is the \textbf{virama}, and it sits under a consonant meaning: \emph{no vowel here.}

Then something happens that no European alphabet does. A consonant stripped of its vowel usually does not sit there bare — it \textbf{fuses} with the consonant after it into one joined shape, a \textbf{conjunct}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{स}} + \textbf{\mr{्}} + \textbf{\mr{क}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{स्क}}
\end{quote}

\emph{ska}, one cluster. Look closely and both letters are still in there. \textbf{Conjuncts are not new characters to memorise} — they are two you already know, joined, and the head-line runs straight across the join.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{्}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the virama do? (\textbf{Removes the inherent vowel}.) What usually happens to a consonant that loses its vowel? (It \textbf{joins} the next into a conjunct.) And are conjuncts new letters? (\textbf{No} — two known letters, fused.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra]{\mr{र} — the last consonant of the greeting}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-ra}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{र}
\end{quote}

\textbf{ra} — a light tap of the tongue, closer to the \emph{r} in Spanish \emph{pero} than to an English \emph{r}.

That is the last piece. Everything the greeting needs is now something you can write from memory.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is \textbf{\mr{र}} made? (A \textbf{light tap} of the tongue, not an English \emph{r}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[namaskār]{\mr{नमस्कार} — seven pieces, all of them already yours}

\label{lesson:MR-W01-namaskar-read}



\begin{quote}
Write the piece from the previous lesson before adding another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Nothing new is introduced in this lesson. Every piece below is one you can write.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{न}} + \textbf{\mr{म}} + \textbf{\mr{स}} + \textbf{\mr{्}} + \textbf{\mr{क}} + \textbf{\mr{ा}} + \textbf{\mr{र}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}}
\end{quote}

Read it the way you built it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{न}} — \emph{na}, inherent vowel
  \item \textbf{\mr{म}} — \emph{ma}, inherent vowel
  \item \textbf{\mr{स्क}} — the conjunct: \emph{sa} with its vowel removed, fused to \emph{ka}
  \item \textbf{\mr{ा}} — the mātrā, making that piece \emph{kā}
  \item \textbf{\mr{र}} — \emph{ra}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{na-ma-skār.} The greeting from your first lesson, now decoded rather than recalled.

Count what it took: \textbf{six consonants, three vowel signs, and one virama.} With them you can read \emph{yes}, \emph{no}, and the greeting — and every consonant you meet from here obeys rules you already hold.

Devanagari has around forty more letters. It does not have any more \textbf{systems}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \mr{नमस्कार}
  \item \emph{Read it:} every piece this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new pieces were in this lesson? (\textbf{None}.) What is \textbf{\mr{स्क}} made of? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{स}}} with its vowel removed, joined to \emph{\textbf{\mr{क}}}.) And what still remains to learn — rules, or shapes? (\textbf{Shapes}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhanyavad]{\mr{धन्यवाद} (dhanyavād) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-dhanyavad}



\begin{quote}
The formal \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{} — Sanskrit, shared across the Indian languages.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} New: \textbf{\mr{ध}} \emph{dha} (a breathy \emph{d}), \textbf{\mr{य}} \emph{ya}, \textbf{\mr{वा}} \emph{vā}, \textbf{\mr{द}} \emph{da}, and the conjunct \textbf{\mr{न्य}} (\emph{na} + \emph{ya}). Read \textbf{\mr{ध}·\mr{न्य}·\mr{वा}·\mr{द}} $\to$ \textbf{dhanyavād}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{धन्यवाद}} (\emph{dhanyavād}) = Sanskrit \emph{dhanya} (\textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}an utterance of '{[}you are{]} worthy.'\textquotedblright{} The same Sanskrit word behind Hindi \emph{dhanyavād}, Kannada \emph{dhanyavāda}, Telugu \emph{dhanyavādamulu}. Warmer, more spoken Marathi often says \textbf{\mr{आभारी} \mr{आहे}} (\emph{ābhārī āhe}, \textquotedblleft{}{[}I{]} am grateful\textquotedblright{}), on the root \emph{ābhār}, \textquotedblleft{}gratitude.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavād\textquotedblright{}
  \item the warmer spoken form — \textquotedblleft{}ābhārī āhe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two Sanskrit pieces of \textbf{\mr{धन्यवाद}}, and a warmer Marathi alternative? (\emph{dhanya} \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{} + \emph{vāda} \textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{}; \emph{ābhārī āhe}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ho]{\mr{हो} (ho) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-ho}



\begin{quote}
A one-syllable \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{ह}} (\emph{ha}) + the \emph{o}-mātrā \textbf{\mr{ो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{हो}} (\emph{ho}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{हो}} (\emph{ho}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) is Marathi's plain affirmative — distinct from Hindi's \emph{hāṁ}. Marathi builds its own everyday words on shared Indo-Aryan roots. The polite, fuller \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} is \emph{ho, baraṃ āhe} (\textquotedblleft{}yes, it's fine\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ho\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{})
  \item the fuller polite form — \textquotedblleft{}ho, baraṃ āhe\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is Marathi's \textquotedblleft{}yes,\textquotedblright{} and how does it differ from Hindi's? (\emph{ho}; Hindi says \emph{hāṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[baram]{\mr{बरं} (baraṃ) — \textquotedblleft{}okay, fine\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-baram}



\begin{quote}
The verbal shrug of Marathi — \textquotedblleft{}sure, fine, all right.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{ब}} (\emph{ba}) + \textbf{\mr{रं}} (\emph{ra} with the \emph{anusvāra} dot \textbf{\mr{ं}}, a light nasal) $\to$ \textbf{baraṃ}. That dot on top nasalises the vowel.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{बरं}} (\emph{baraṃ}, \textquotedblleft{}okay, fine, good, all right\textquotedblright{}) is the oil of everyday Marathi talk — a soft \textquotedblleft{}sure, fine.\textquotedblright{} Its neutral form is \emph{bare}. A genuinely Marathi word, not a Sanskrit loan — the kind of small, high-frequency word that gives a language its everyday texture.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}baraṃ\textquotedblright{} (feel the nasal dot)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ho, baraṃ āhe\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}yes, it's fine\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{बरं}} mean, and what does the dot \textbf{\mr{ं}} do? (\textquotedblleft{}Okay/fine\textquotedblright{}; the anusvāra nasalises the vowel.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nahi]{\mr{नाही} (nāhī) — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} a word older than English}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-nahi}



\begin{quote}
The partner of \emph{ho} — built on one of the oldest words in the whole Indo-European family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{ना}} (\emph{nā}) + \textbf{\mr{ही}} (\emph{hī}) $\to$ \textbf{nāhī}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{नाही}} (\emph{nāhī}, \textquotedblleft{}no / is not\textquotedblright{}) sits on the ancient negative \textbf{na-} — the \emph{same} Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}, Latin \emph{non}, and Hindi \emph{nahīṁ}. So Marathi's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} and English's \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} are cousins from before either language existed. It doubles as \textquotedblleft{}there isn't\textquotedblright{}: Marathi, like Hindi, denies with this one word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \emph{ho} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) / \emph{nāhī} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{})
  \item the ancient cousins — \emph{no}, \emph{not}, Latin \emph{non}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ancient root is \textbf{\mr{नाही}} built on, and what English words share it? (PIE \emph{*ne}; \emph{no}, \emph{not}, \emph{none}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yeto / yete]{\mr{येतो} / \mr{येते} (yeto / yete) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll take my leave\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-yeto}



\begin{quote}
The Marathi goodbye — which, like the Dravidian languages, refuses to say a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{} And it changes with the speaker's gender.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{ये}} (\emph{ye}) + \textbf{\mr{तो}} (\emph{to}) $\to$ \emph{yeto}; \textbf{\mr{ये}} + \textbf{\mr{ते}} (\emph{te}) $\to$ \emph{yete}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Marathi, like the Dravidian languages to its south, will not say a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{} The everyday goodbye is \textbf{\mr{येतो}} (\emph{yeto}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{come} {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} a promise of return, never a final departure. (Fuller: \emph{yeto, namaskār}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Marathi verbs carry gender}]
\emph{yeto} is what a \textbf{man} says; a \textbf{woman} says \textbf{\mr{येते}} (\emph{yete}). The verb itself changes with the speaker's gender — something Hindi does only in the past tense, but Marathi does in the \textbf{present} too. (And Marathi keeps \textbf{three} genders — masculine, feminine, and neuter — where Hindi kept only two.) You'll meet this at every verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}yeto\textquotedblright{} (if male) / \textquotedblleft{}yete\textquotedblright{} (if female)
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}I come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}) — a promise of return
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Marathi goodbye literally mean, and why two forms? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}; the verb agrees with the speaker's gender — \emph{yeto} m. / \emph{yete} f.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — recap}

\label{lesson:MR-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}} & \emph{namaskār} & hello / goodbye \\
\textbf{\mr{धन्यवाद}} & \emph{dhanyavād} & thank you \\
\textbf{\mr{हो}} & \emph{ho} & yes \\
\textbf{\mr{नाही}} & \emph{nāhī} & no \\
\textbf{\mr{बरं}} & \emph{baraṃ} & okay / fine \\
\textbf{\mr{येतो} / \mr{येते}} & \emph{yeto / yete} & \textquotedblleft{}I'll be going\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item It prefers \textbf{namaskār} as the everyday greeting (Hindi leans on \emph{namaste}).
  \item It keeps \textbf{three} genders — masculine, feminine, neuter — where Hindi kept two.
  \item It marks \textbf{gender on the verb}, even in the present: \emph{yeto} (m.) / \emph{yete} (f.).
  \item It has an \textbf{extra letter, \mr{ळ}} (retroflex \emph{ḷ}), shared with the Dravidian south and absent from Hindi.
\end{itemize}

Shared with Hindi/Sanskrit: the Devanagari script, the negative \emph{nā-} ($\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne}, English \emph{no}), and much formal vocabulary (\emph{dhanyavād}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six — namaskār · dhanyavād · ho · nāhī · baraṃ · yeto/yete
  \item greet and thank — \textquotedblleft{}namaskār!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavād.\textquotedblright{}
  \item your leave-taking — \textquotedblleft{}yeto/yete\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}}, write \textbf{\mr{हो}} once without a model, then name two ways Marathi differs from Hindi despite sharing Devanagari. (Prefers \emph{namaskār}; three genders; gender on the verb; the extra letter \emph{\mr{ळ}}.)

Next chapter: introducing yourself — \emph{mājhe nāv…} (\textquotedblleft{}my name…\textquotedblright{}) — and Marathi's \emph{tū} / \emph{tumhī} (familiar / respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}).
\end{tcolorbox}
